#### 0. Loading Necessary Packages 
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(purrr)

set.seed(1)
```

#### Problem 1. 
```{r problem-1-plot}

bday = function(n) {
  bdays = sample.int(365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  dup = length(unique(bdays)) < n
  
  return(dup)
}

bday_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    n = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    duplicate = map_lgl(n, bday)
  ) |>
  group_by(n) |>
  summarize(
    probability = mean(duplicate)
  )

bday_results_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = probability)) + 
  geom_line()
    
```

Probability that at least two people in a group with share the same birthday increases as group size increases. There are steep increases in probability between n = 10 and around n = 30. The probability of a duplicate birthday crosses the 50% mark when the group size is  `r bday_results_df |> filter(probability > 0.50) |> pull(n) |> min()` These steep increases start to flatten as group size approaches n = 50. When the group size is 50 individuals, the probability simulated is close to 100%, at `r bday_results_df |> filter(n==50) |> pull(probability) * 100`%.

#### Problem 2

_Creating a dataframe containing all file names_
```{r, problem-2-plot, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
prob_2_data = tibble(
  files = list.files("./data")
) |>
  mutate(path = str_c("./data/", files),
       data = map(path, read_csv)
       ) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  separate(files, into = c("arm", "id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    id = str_remove(id, "\\.csv"), 
    arm = case_match(arm,
                     "con" ~ "control",
                     "exp" ~ "experimental")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = week_1:week_8,
    names_prefix = "week_",
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |>
  select(-path) |> 
  relocate(id)

prob_2_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, color = arm, group = interaction(arm, id))) + 
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = "μ"
  )
  
```

At week one, the two study arms start out similarly. Over the 8 weeks, observation values in the experimental arm increase. The observations in the control arm stay flat over the observation period. By the end of the observation period, the control and experimental arm's observations are separated, with all observations in the experimental arm higher than the controls.


#### Problem 3

_Creating t test function, and iterating 5000 times with $\mu$ = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6_
```{r}

#t test output: estimate is our mu hat here

sim_ttest = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )
  
  t.test(sim_data |> pull(x), mu = 0) |> 
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

sim_ttest_df = 
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    t_test_results = map(mu, sim_ttest)
  ) |>
  unnest(t_test_results)

```

_Plot showing proportion of times the null was rejected_
```{r, problem-3-plot-a}
sim_ttest_df |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(power = mean(p.value < 0.05)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) + 
  geom_line()
```

As the effect size increases, statistical power increases. We are more likely to reject the null hypothesis at $\mu$ = 6 than $\mu$ = 0. 

_Plot showing average estimate of $\hat{\mu}$ on y axis and true value of $\hat{\mu}$ on the x axis + plot of the average estimate of $\hat{\mu}$ only in samples for which the null was rejected_

```{r, problem-3-plot-b}
sim_ttest_df |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    avg = mean(estimate),
    avg_rej = mean(estimate[p.value < 0.05])
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = avg, color = "All")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = avg_rej, color = "Where the null was rejected")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = avg, color = "All"))+
  geom_point(aes(y = avg_rej, color = "Where the null was rejected")) +
  labs(x = "True value of μ",
       y = expression("Average estimate of " * hat(mu)),
       color = "Samples")

```

The sample average of $\hat{\mu}$ is approximately equal to the true value of $\mu$ when all observations, even those where we fail to reject the null, are included in our calculation. In contrast, when we only include samples where the null is rejected, $\hat{\mu}$ is greater than the true mean when $\mu$ is 0, 1, 2, and 3. As we saw in the previous plot, when $\mu$ is small, the power of the test is also small. So, unusually large $\hat{\mu}$'s would be the only ones that typically reach significance. For $\mu$ between 4 and 6, the power is near 1, and so nearly all sample nulls are rejected, making the estimated $\hat{\mu}$ match the true $\mu$.
